Chapter 27

The remote form

SvelteKit 3's form() — a server function you import into a component, that works with JavaScript disabled.

By the end of this chapter

A typed, validated, progressively-enhanced signup with no hand-written API endpoint.

This is the flagship SvelteKit 3 feature. A remote function runs only on the server, but you import it into a component as if it were local. SvelteKit replaces the import with a fetch call at build time.

You get one typed function signature spanning client and server. No hand-written endpoint, no fetch('/api/…'), no manually maintained request and response types.

The file must have a .remote.ts suffix. That is not a convention you could rename — SvelteKit looks for that segment specifically.

Why form() and not command()

The whole reason

A command() fires from an event handler and needs JavaScript. A form() is spread onto a real <form> element, so it submits as an ordinary HTTP POST when JavaScript has not loaded, has failed, or is disabled — then progressively enhances itself once hydrated. For the most important conversion point on the site, working without JavaScript is not a nice-to-have.

The schema

Checkbox fields must be optional. An unchecked checkbox sends *nothing* — not false, the field is simply absent. So v.boolean() can never be satisfied by an unchecked box. SvelteKit enforces this at the type level: write a non-optional boolean and the form() overload resolves to a string literal explaining the problem, and your handler stops type-checking. It is a deliberately designed compile error, and a much better teacher than a runtime bug where consent silently never validates.

The leading underscore on _company is a SvelteKit convention: fields whose names start with _ are not repopulated into the form when validation fails. It exists for passwords, and suits a honeypot too.

Why Valibot rather than Zod

Both implement the Standard Schema spec, which is the interface SvelteKit accepts here — so either drops in unchanged. Valibot tree-shakes: you ship only the validators you import, which for this form is a few hundred bytes rather than Zod's ~13kB. On a marketing page where bundle size is a ranking input, that is worth having.

The handler

Why the bot gets a success page

Returning "bot detected" hands the author of the bot a free test harness for evading your check. We behave exactly as if the signup succeeded, and simply do not store anything.

Why 303 and not 302

303 (See Other) tells the browser to follow up with a GET. That is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern, and it is what stops a browser refresh from resubmitting the form and creating a duplicate.

redirect() throws. Nothing after that line runs — which is what you want, and also why you must never wrap a redirect in a try/catch that swallows everything. The catch eats the redirect and the user sits on the form wondering what happened. This is a genuinely common bug.

Server-side validation is the only validation that counts. Client-side checks are a convenience for honest users; anyone can bypass them with curl. Never treat them as a security boundary.

Checkpoint

pnpm run check passes. If it complains about the form() overload, your consent field is not optional — re-read the warning above.
